The best questions gently force others to look at the assumptions underlying their views and examine the thinking and feelings just below the smooth surface.
Carefully worded questions have the potential to open up conversations rather than shutting them down.

Instead, they understand the power of a curious but challenging question to promote open dialogue, engender the exploration of ideas, and to teach people how to think more critically. Exceptional leaders are always teachers.

t: The Effort and Efficacy Beliefs
q: The Effort belief is absent when you don't think you can improve.
But when a student thinks Effort is something detached from their ability to improve, make no mistake: that is a student inflicted with Effort unbelief.
It's hard to overstate how powerfully our beliefs about our Efficacy predict our performance.
You hear a lot of people saying, I'm a growth mindset person, but it turns out that we're all a mixture, often depending on the environment we're in.
Valorizing ineffective Effort sends a signal to students that school is a bizarre place where outcomes don't matter—all that matters is that you try.
All human beings want to be motivated. This student does, too. There's just something getting in the way right now—something that you get to work at puzzling out.

t: Team Members Over-Interpret the Actions of a New Leader
q: team members engage in an active hunt for meaning in everything the new leader does.
In the search for meaning and certainty, team members make big inferences from the small acts and choices a new leader makes.
Since leaders can’t prevent team members from drawing conclusions about their often random choices, they have the opportunity to become more intentional about what they do.
Whatever is most important (initiatives, people, customers, issues) should come first on purpose.
Team members have a need to predict how the leader will engage in the future and will continually draw inferences from nearly all actions and choices during the honeymoon phase.

t: #68 Make Groups Explicitly Random and Change Them Regularly
q: If groups remain consistent over time, students are likely to fall into certain roles within a group. One or two students always lead the thinking, while other students in the group adopt the role of passengers.
Changing the groups regularly—Liljedahl recommends doing this every lesson - means each group provides an opportunity to start afresh.
Students always have a suspicion as to why they have been put into a particular group - oh, I am not as smart as those guys, so my job is to be a passenger.
Even if you genuinely do randomly allocate the groups, students are unlikely to believe it is random. So, they need showing.
Liljedahl recommends asking students to pick a card from a deck upon entry to the classroom and then sit on the table corresponding to the number on their card.
Of course, allocating the groups is just the tip of the iceberg in terms of getting group work right, but thinking about it is an interesting place to start.
